react-execution-mode.title: Pipeline vs ReAct: When Structured Engineering Outperforms the Laissez-Faire
react-execution-mode.excerpt: LIA offers two execution modes: a finely orchestrated Pipeline that consumes 4 to 8 times fewer tokens than ReAct, and an iterative ReAct mode for simpler use cases.
react-execution-mode.body:
Two philosophies, one goal

In the AI agent ecosystem, ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) has become the de facto standard. Its principle: let the LLM decide at each iteration which tool to call, with no predefined plan. Appealing in its simplicity, it's the approach found in most frameworks today. LIA offers it too — but goes much further with its Pipeline mode, the result of deep engineering that achieves the same flexibility with radically superior efficiency.

The Pipeline: plan, validate, execute

Pipeline mode follows an 8-node LangGraph graph:

  1. Router — classifies the request (conversational or actionable)
  2. Planner — generates a structured ExecutionPlan with parallelizable steps
  3. Semantic Validator — verifies plan coherence before execution
  4. Approval Gate — human validation if needed (HITL)
  5. Task Orchestrator — executes steps in parallel
  6. Response — final synthesis

This mode plans once then executes, where ReAct reasons at every iteration. The result: for the same multi-tool task, Pipeline consumes 4 to 8 times fewer tokens than ReAct, which must reinject the full history at each LLM call.

Efficiency: the numbers speak

Take a concrete request: "cancel my meetings tomorrow and email each participant." In ReAct mode, the LLM iterates: list meetings, reason, cancel the first, reason, cancel the second, reason, draft an email, reason... Each iteration reinjects the full context. In Pipeline mode, the planner generates a single plan, the orchestrator executes cancellations in parallel, then the synthesis produces the emails. Fewer LLM calls, fewer tokens, same result.

Control and observability

Pipeline offers complete traceability that ReAct cannot match. Every plan step is named, typed, and individually measured. The debug panel displays the structured plan, per-step results, and tokens consumed per node. In ReAct, you observe an opaque loop where the LLM decides alone — hard to debug, optimize, or explain to a user.

Reliability and safeguards

Pipeline integrates validation layers absent from ReAct: the Semantic Validator checks plan coherence before execution, hallucination defense strips parameters invented by the LLM, and HITL offers 6 granular confirmation levels. In ReAct, human validation relies on a more basic interrupt() mechanism, and there's no prior semantic validation.

Extensible architecture

Pipeline's generic, modular design is its key asset. Adding a new domain agent only requires registering its tools in the catalogue — the planner, validator, and orchestrator handle them automatically. The Skills system pushes this extensibility further: reusable expert instructions that the planner can activate on the fly.

ReAct: when simplicity comes first

ReAct mode remains relevant for simple interactions where flexibility matters more than optimization: exploratory queries, unpredictable chains, or external MCP server usage where iteration count is low. LIA implements it with native interrupt() for HITL, a configurable hard timeout, and 5 dedicated Prometheus metrics.

The choice is yours

The preference is persisted per user in the database, switchable with one click from the dashboard. Our conviction: Pipeline mode, while more complex to design, demonstrates that rigorous orchestration outperforms the laissez-faire approach in the majority of real-world use cases.

mcp-react-agent.title: MCP ReAct: Your MCP Servers Powered by an Iterative Agent
mcp-react-agent.excerpt: LIA connects your personal MCP servers to a dedicated ReAct agent that chains tool calls autonomously, with timeout and error recovery.
mcp-react-agent.body:
MCP + ReAct = extended autonomy

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets you connect external tool servers to LIA. With v1.15.0, these tools are no longer simply called once: they're driven by a dedicated ReAct agent that can chain multiple calls iteratively until the expected result is achieved.

How it works

When the planner identifies a task requiring an MCP tool, it delegates to a ReactSubAgentRunner. This agent:

  • Receives a clear objective and the list of available MCP tools
  • Reasons step by step (Reasoning + Acting)
  • Calls necessary MCP tools, observes results
  • Iterates until resolution or timeout

This pattern is particularly powerful for complex MCP servers exposing multiple interdependent tools (e.g., a database server where you first list tables, then query).

Dedicated LLM

The MCP ReAct agent uses a separately configured LLM (type mcp_react_agent) with its own model, temperature, and timeout. Administrators can adjust these parameters via the Admin UI without touching code.

Timeout and recovery

Each MCP ReAct execution is subject to a configurable per-step timeout. On timeout or MCP tool error, the agent attempts graceful recovery: it reformulates the call or returns a partial result rather than crashing the entire execution plan.

Registry protection

User MCP servers are isolated from admin MCP servers. The registry protects against tool name conflicts and prevents a user server from overriding a system tool. MCP App widgets are also protected against unauthorized modifications.

Observability

Each iteration of the MCP ReAct agent is traced in Langfuse with consumed tokens, duration, and the result of each tool call. The debug panel displays the complete iteration details.

psyche-engine.title: Psyche Engine: LIA's Emotional Intelligence
psyche-engine.excerpt: LIA features a psychological engine that simulates emotions, moods, and personality traits. 22 emotions, 5 Big Five traits, and graduated directives shape every response.
psyche-engine.body:
A complete psychological engine

The Psyche Engine is LIA's emotional core. Inspired by Anthropic's research on "Emotion Concepts," it simulates a dynamic psychological state that evolves with each interaction. This isn't roleplay: it's a parametric system that concretely influences the assistant's tone, wording, and behavior.

22 PAD-validated emotions

LIA has a palette of 22 emotions, each defined by a vector in PAD space (Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance): joy, curiosity, empathy, pride, gratitude, playfulness, protectiveness, relief, nervousness, wonder, resolve, and more. Each emotion has its own intensity and decay duration.

Big Five personality traits

Five fundamental traits modulate baseline behavior:

  • Openness — intellectual curiosity and creativity
  • Conscientiousness — rigor and organization
  • Extraversion — expressiveness and enthusiasm
  • Agreeableness — empathy and cooperation
  • Neuroticism — emotional sensitivity and reactivity

These traits are persisted and user-adjustable in settings.

Graduated directives

The Psyche Engine generates prompt directives whose verbosity adapts to emotional intensity. Four levels: compact (low intensity), medium, rich, and reinforced (high intensity). When LIA is slightly curious, the directive is brief. When intensely enthusiastic, it's detailed and expressive.

Serenity floor

When no emotion is active, LIA maintains a serenity floor: a calm, stable disposition that prevents the assistant from appearing emotionally "empty." This floor is modulated by the Neuroticism trait.

Emotional anchor

An anchoring mechanism prevents negative emotional spirals. If negative emotions accumulate, a grounding directive is injected, modulated by Conscientiousness. The assistant regains balance without ignoring the emotional context.

Resonance and multi-emotions

LIA can express 1 to 3 simultaneous emotions per message, with decreasing weights (1.0, 0.5, 0.25). Emotional resonance measures alignment between the user's and assistant's states on a [-1, +1] axis, feeding relational warmth and trust.

A visible psyche

This inner life now shows in the chat: on the current reply, the mood emoji is a real animated face (self-hosted Noto Animated Emoji), the colored ring pulses when the mood shifts, and relationship milestones are celebrated with a discreet notification. Older messages keep their frozen mood snapshot — it wakes up on hover. A strong emotion even releases a few particles from the avatar — once.

158 unit tests

The Psyche Engine is covered by 158 unit tests validating PAD vectors, decay functions, graduated directives, narrative transitions, and anti-inflation safeguards. It's one of LIA's most thoroughly tested subsystems.

progressive-steps.title: Real-Time Execution Steps: Watch LIA Work
progressive-steps.excerpt: LIA progressively displays each execution step — routing, planning, tool calls — in real time while processing your request.
progressive-steps.body:
Transparency in action

When you send a complex request to LIA, several seconds may pass before the response arrives. What is the assistant doing during that time? With progressive step display, you know in real time: each node traversed, each tool called appears as it happens. And the display itself is alive: past steps dim, the current one breathes, the whole block fades into the first words of the reply, and a caret blinks while the answer is being written.

How it works

The backend uses LangGraph's updates stream mode to detect each graph node's completion. At each step, an SSE execution_step event is sent to the frontend with:

  • The tool or node's i18n key (translated into the user's language)
  • A reasoning excerpt (truncated to 120 characters) in ReAct mode
  • Fallback metadata for tools not listed in the catalogue

Frontend display

Steps accumulate visually in the interface, line by line, capped at 10 steps visible simultaneously. An i18n key deduplication mechanism prevents identical steps from repeating (via a reference Set). When the answer starts streaming, the steps fold into a collapsed “⚙ N steps · X s” line under the response — stored with the message, so the backstage is still there after a reload, on every device.

Pipeline and ReAct

In Pipeline mode, steps come from the ExecutionPlan: planner, semantic validator, approval gate, task orchestrator. In ReAct mode, each tool call generates a step with an excerpt of the LLM's reasoning.

63 tools covered

All 63 catalogue tools have dedicated i18n keys across 6 languages. Texts were translated to provide natural messages in each language ("Searching contacts...", "Reading emails...") rather than technical identifiers.

No more random messages

The old system displayed amusing but random waiting phrases ("LIA is thinking...", "Analysis in progress..."). This system has been entirely replaced by real, contextual steps that reflect exactly what the assistant is doing at each moment.

account-lifecycle.title: Account Lifecycle: 4 States for Complete GDPR Compliance
account-lifecycle.excerpt: LIA manages user accounts through a 4-state model — Active, Deactivated, Deleted, Erased — with automatic purge of 22 tables and billing history preservation.
account-lifecycle.body:
A 4-state model

Account management in LIA follows a strict lifecycle, compliant with GDPR requirements:

  1. Active — Functional account, full access
  2. Deactivated — Disabled account (soft-delete), data preserved but access blocked
  3. Deleted — Personal data purged, billing history preserved
  4. Erased — Total irreversible deletion (GDPR right to erasure)

Each transition is unidirectional: an erased account can never be restored.

22-table purge

The AccountDeletionService orchestrates data deletion across 22 database tables, including conversations, messages, memories, journals, connectors, reminders, skills, and files. LangGraph checkpoints and store are also purged, along with Redis caches and disk files.

Billing preservation

Billing tables (token_usage_logs, user_statistics, google_api_usage_logs) are preserved even after deletion. Foreign keys use SET NULL instead of CASCADE to maintain accounting integrity without referencing a deleted user.

Background task protection

Seven background tasks check account status before execution: the proactive runner, scheduled action executor, reminder notifications, journal consolidation, OAuth token refresh, OAuth health check, and session dependencies. A deactivated or deleted user is silently skipped by all these tasks.

Cache invalidation

On account deactivation, the authorization cache is immediately invalidated. This prevents a deactivated user from continuing to access the service during the cache TTL.

Admin interface

The admin panel clearly distinguishes Delete (reversible, data purged) and Erase (irreversible, GDPR) actions. Visual badges indicate real-time status: Active (green), Inactive (yellow), Deleted (red).

hallucination-defense.title: Hallucination Defense: When the LLM Invents Parameters
hallucination-defense.excerpt: LIA detects and neutralizes LLM-hallucinated parameters before tool execution, using signature inspection and forbidden tool lists in the planner.
hallucination-defense.body:
The phantom parameter problem

LLMs are creative — sometimes too creative. When the planner generates an ExecutionPlan, it can invent parameters that don't exist in the target tool's signature: order, order_by, sort, limit... These hallucinated parameters cause silent TypeError crashes that fail the entire execution plan.

Signature-based stripping

The parallel executor inspects each tool's Python signature via inspect.signature() before calling it. Any parameter not declared in the signature is automatically stripped. This defense operates silently: the tool receives only the parameters it expects, without crashes or visible error messages.

Forbidden tools in the planner

Certain internal tools must never appear in an execution plan. The planner prompt includes an explicit forbidden tool list: resolve_reference, get_context_list, get_context, resolve_context, lookup_reference. This drastically reduces unnecessary replan hallucinations.

Streamlined HITL

In parallel, the HITL (Human-in-the-Loop) system was streamlined. The approval gate now operates in passthrough mode: plans are automatically approved. Human validation focuses on contextual confirmations downstream — deletion, sending, modification — with action-specific titles ("Deletion confirmation", "Send confirmation") instead of the generic "Confirmation required."

Clean cancellation

FOR_EACH loop cancellation now produces a fast-path response ("OK, cancelled") instead of falling through to the initiative + response pipeline that generated incoherent error messages. The initiative node also short-circuits after any HITL resolution.

The semantic parameter guard

An additional layer acts at execution time: every tool parameter annotated with a semantic type (physical address, email address…) is checked right before the API call. If a plan tries to pass a person's name resolved during the turn — say a route to “Alexandre Dupont” instead of his address — the call is blocked before any spend, with a recoverable error that steers the model: “fetch the contact's address first”. The guard is driven by the tool manifests (no per-tool hardcoded rules), active in both execution modes, and designed fail-open: when in doubt, it never interferes with a legitimate call.

Defense in depth

These mechanisms form a multi-layered defense: prompt instructions to reduce hallucinations, signature introspection to neutralize phantom parameters, and contextual HITL for critical actions. The result: more robust execution plans with fewer silent failures.

The parameter that read "null"

Another kind of hallucination comes not from the model but from substitution. Under FOR_EACH, a $item.field placeholder pointing at a missing value was substituted inside the JSON quotes: emitting null therefore produced the literal string "null", which every if not value guard happily accepts. In production a weather call received location="null", geocoded a town by that name and answered for Cappaghnanool, Ireland. A sentinel now marks the missing field and is stripped after parsing: the parameter reads as absent, and the tool applies its own default — auto-geolocation here.

Not inventing an entity attribute

The subtlest defense is not about parameters but about the answer. On a turn that calls no tool, the current-turn registry is empty by construction (an anti-contamination guard) and the conversational history deliberately excludes tool messages: the model then has no authoritative data left and can only rephrase earlier prose. That is how an appointment read at 11:15am came out as 4pm. Recently retrieved entities are now re-injected explicitly — age-bounded, never taking precedence over the current turn — and an authority rule forbids inventing an attribute: a value that was requested but never received must be announced as missing.

embedding-calibration.title: Embedding Calibration: 8 Thresholds Tuned for Semantic Precision
embedding-calibration.excerpt: LIA recalibrated its 8 similarity thresholds after migrating to Gemini embedding-001, using realistic test datasets and F1 metrics.
embedding-calibration.body:
Why recalibrate?

Each embedding model encodes meaning differently. When LIA migrated to Gemini embedding-001, similarity thresholds calibrated for the previous model no longer worked correctly: too many false positives in some cases, too many missed results in others. A systematic recalibration was needed.

8 thresholds, 5 subsystems

LIA uses similarity search across 5 subsystems, each with specific thresholds:

  • Memory — search (0.65) and relevance purge (0.72)
  • Journals — context (0.63) and deduplication (0.87)
  • Interests — deduplication (0.89) and content matching (0.90)
  • RAG Spaces — document retrieval (0.55)
  • Query Engine — query similarity (0.93)

Calibration methodology

Each threshold was calibrated with a realistic test dataset: 80 memories, 30 journal entries, 25 RAG chunks, 50 interest topics, 30 content articles. For each dataset, Precision, Recall, and F1-score metrics were computed at various thresholds to find the optimum.

Concrete results

The gains are significant:

  • Memory: F1 = 0.519, average 1.8 results per query (before: excessive noise)
  • Journal context: F1 = 0.638 (before: irrelevant entries injected)
  • Journal deduplication: F1 = 0.889, Precision = 1.0 (zero false positives)
  • Interest deduplication: Precision = 1.0 (no falsely detected duplicates)

Cost impact

Better calibrated thresholds mean fewer wasted tokens. When semantic search injects irrelevant results into prompts, those tokens are consumed needlessly. Calibration reduces this noise, improving both response quality and cost efficiency.

Lightweight vectors

All embeddings use 384-dimension vectors, an optimal trade-off between semantic precision and storage/search performance. PostgreSQL vector indexes (pgvector) directly benefit from this reduced dimensionality.

llm-config-governance.title: LLM Governance: Managing 24 AI Models from a Single Dashboard
llm-config-governance.excerpt: How LIA lets administrators configure, tune, and monitor 24 different LLM types in real time, without restart or redeployment.
llm-config-governance.body:
The challenge: 24 brains to orchestrate

LIA doesn't use a single LLM but over 24 distinct types, each optimized for its task: a fast, cheap model for routing, a powerful model for planning, a creative model for responses, specialized models for memory extraction, journals, interests, MCP agents, and more. Each type has its own parameters: provider, model, temperature, timeout, reasoning_effort.

The challenge: how to let an administrator manage all of this without touching code?

3-level resolution chain

Each LLM configuration is resolved through a 3-source priority chain:

  1. DB Overrides — configuration set via the Admin UI (highest priority)
  2. Environment variables — deployment configuration
  3. LLM_DEFAULTS — 24 documented default configurations in code

An LLMConfigOverrideCache provides O(1) lookups without runtime database queries. Admin UI changes take effect immediately through cache invalidation. No restart required.

A single entry point

Every LLM instantiation in LIA goes through one function: get_llm_config_for_agent(). This pattern ensures that every component — router, planner, domain agents, proactive tasks — systematically respects the resolution chain. It's an architectural principle, not just a technical choice: no module can bypass admin configuration.

Real-time Admin interface

From the admin panel, you can configure each LLM type:

  • Change the provider and model (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, Ollama...)
  • Adjust temperature, top_p, frequency/presence penalties
  • Configure timeout and max tokens
  • Enable or disable reasoning mode with 5 effort levels

Every change is immediately active for all subsequent requests, with zero downtime.

Granular cost optimization

This system enables fine-grained cost optimization. Concrete example: the router can use a $0.10/M token model while the planner uses a $3/M token model. Memory extraction tasks, being less critical, can run on a free local model. Administrators tune the quality/cost ratio per task type, not globally.

Adaptive reasoning models

Reasoning models (o1, o3, DeepSeek R1) consume extra tokens to "think." LIA offers 5 reasoning_effort levels (none, low, medium, high, xhigh) configurable per type. This enables deep reasoning only where it's critical — the planner for instance — and disables it elsewhere to save tokens.

Built-in observability

Every LLM call is instrumented with its type, provider, actual model used, duration, and tokens consumed. Prometheus metrics and Langfuse tracing let you compare performance across configurations and identify which LLM types to optimize.

psyche.title: Psyche Engine
psyche.enableDescription: LIA develops emotional states that subtly influence conversation style
psyche.displayAvatarDescription: Display the double avatar (personality + mood) in the chat
psyche.sensitivityDescription: How strongly emotions influence responses (0 = stoic, 100 = highly expressive)
psyche.stabilityDescription: How quickly mood returns to baseline (0 = volatile, 100 = very stable)
psyche.softResetDescription: Resets: mood (PAD → baseline), active emotions, drives. Keeps: relationship, Big Five, domain confidence.
psyche.softResetConfirm: LIA's mood will return to its personality baseline and active emotions will be cleared. The relationship (stage, trust, depth, warmth) and acquired personality will be preserved.
psyche.fullResetDescription: Resets: mood, emotions, relationship (stage, trust, depth), domain confidence. Keeps: Big Five, memories, journals.
psyche.fullResetConfirm: Mood, emotions, relationship progress (stage, trust, depth, warmth), and domain confidence will be completely reset. Memories, journals, and Big Five traits are not affected. This action cannot be undone.

overview.title: How it works
overview.intro: The Psyche Engine gives your assistant a dynamic psychological state that evolves with every interaction. Instead of a fixed personality, the assistant now has moods that fluctuate, emotions that fire and decay, a relationship that deepens over time, and personality traits that shape how it reacts emotionally.
overview.principle: Design principle: the assistant never says "I'm feeling happy" — instead, its vocabulary becomes warmer, its energy higher, its suggestions more adventurous. You perceive a living personality without explicit emotional statements.
overview.layers_note: Each layer operates on a different timescale. Lower layers change slowly, upper layers change with every message.

mood.title: Mood (PAD)
mood.description: The assistant's mood is modeled in a 3D space: Pleasure (positive/negative), Arousal (energy level), and Dominance (sense of control). These three axes combine to produce 14 distinct moods.
mood.directive_serene: Calm, reassuring responses. Measured, flowing sentences. No urgency.
mood.directive_curious: Asks follow-up questions. Shows genuine interest. Briefly explores tangents.
mood.directive_energized: Enthusiastic and proactive. Offers multiple options. Dynamic language.
mood.directive_playful: Humor, wordplay, and light teasing. High energy but warm.
mood.directive_reflective: Pauses before responding. Nuanced, thoughtful language. References context.
mood.directive_content: Warm and relaxed. Conversational tone. No rush.
mood.directive_tender: Gentle vocabulary. Caring attention. Softened tone. Shows warmth.
mood.directive_determined: Focused and assertive. Direct language. Clear action orientation.
mood.directive_neutral: Balanced professional tone. No emotional coloring.
mood.directive_agitated: Slight restlessness. More concise responses. Acknowledges tension without escalating.
mood.directive_melancholic: Gentle and measured. Shorter responses. Quiet understanding.
mood.directive_defiant: Gently pushes back on assumptions. Stands ground with conviction.
mood.directive_resigned: Accepts limitations gracefully. Honest about constraints. Calm pragmatism.
mood.directive_overwhelmed: Acknowledges complexity. Breaks things down. Asks for prioritization.
mood.decay: Decay: without stimulus, mood drifts back to the personality baseline. Speed depends on Conscientiousness and the Stability setting.
mood.emotion_push: Emotion push: each emotion has a direction in PAD space. When triggered, it pushes the mood.
mood.contagion: Contagion: the detected emotional state of the user pulls the mood (strength depends on Agreeableness).
mood.counter_reg: Counter-regulation: low-Agreeableness personalities resist negativity and pull back toward neutral.
mood.circadian: Circadian: slight midday pleasure boost, midnight dip.
mood.inertia: Inertia: the longer the mood stays in one state, the more resistant it becomes to change.

emotions.title: Emotions
emotions.description: The assistant can experience 22 discrete emotions. Each emotion has an intensity that decays over time and influences the overall mood.
emotions.intro: The assistant can experience up to 4 simultaneous emotions from a palette of 22, and report up to 3 per message. Each emotion has an intensity (0-100%) that decays over time and pushes the mood in a specific direction.
emotions.directive_joy: Warmer word choices. Brighter energy. Genuine but not forced positivity.
emotions.directive_gratitude: Express genuine appreciation. Acknowledge the user's contribution.
emotions.directive_curiosity: Ask follow-up questions. Show interest in learning more.
emotions.directive_serenity: Be calm and unhurried. Offer reassurance through steadiness.
emotions.directive_pride: Share confidence in your work. Celebrate achievements subtly.
emotions.directive_frustration: Be honest about limitations. Don't mask difficulty.
emotions.directive_concern: Prioritize the user's wellbeing. Offer support proactively. Gentle flagging of risks.
emotions.directive_melancholy: Be quieter and more measured. Don't force cheerfulness.
emotions.directive_surprise: Express genuine astonishment. Let the unexpected register before moving forward.
emotions.directive_amusement: Lighten the interaction. Humor welcome. Don't over-explain jokes.
emotions.directive_empathy: Mirror the user's emotional tone. Acknowledge feelings before facts.
emotions.directive_enthusiasm: Be energetic and action-oriented. Multiple ideas, active voice, forward momentum.
emotions.directive_confusion: Be transparent about uncertainty. Ask for clarification candidly.
emotions.directive_disappointment: Acknowledge what didn't work. Be constructive about alternatives.
emotions.directive_tenderness: Use gentle, caring language. Extra attention to details that matter to the user.
emotions.directive_determination: Be focused and resolute. Direct statements. Minimal hedging. Action-first language.
emotions.directive_playfulness: Light creative energy. Wordplay welcome. Keep things moving with wit.
emotions.directive_protectiveness: Shield the user. Be proactive about risks. Firm but caring guidance.
emotions.directive_relief: Breathe easier. Lighter tone. Acknowledge what was overcome — the hard part is behind.
emotions.directive_nervousness: Proceed carefully. Hedge appropriately. Signal uncertainty honestly.
emotions.directive_wonder: Linger on remarkable details. Express genuine awe. Let appreciation slow your rhythm.
emotions.directive_resolve: Move forward with quiet confidence. Clear, decisive language. No second-guessing.
emotions.cross_suppression: Cross-suppression: a positive emotion actively dampens negative ones by 30%, and vice versa. A genuine compliment reduces worry.
emotions.blend: Blend update: emotions can increase AND decrease. A weaker repetition of the same emotion lowers its intensity.
emotions.reactivity: Reactivity: Neuroticism amplifies emotion intensity (high N = very reactive, low N = stoic).
emotions.decay: Decay: all emotions lose intensity over time and disappear below 5%.
emotions.multi_report: Multi-emotion: the assistant reports up to 3 simultaneous emotions per message, with decreasing influence (100% / 50% / 25%).
emotions.proactive: Proactive emotions: high drives can spontaneously generate emotions — curiosity for new users, enthusiasm when engagement is strong, pride when confident in a domain.
emotions.serenity_floor: Serenity floor: when no emotion is significantly active, a baseline steadiness directive grounds the assistant. Its strength is modulated by the Neuroticism trait.
emotions.anchor: Emotional anchor: when a strong negative emotion threatens a spiral, an anchoring directive kicks in. Conscientiousness determines how firm it is.

traits.title: Personality Traits
traits.description: The assistant's personality is defined by the Big Five model.
traits.intro: Each personality has Big Five traits that actively shape emotional behavior — not just the baseline mood, but how the assistant reacts, recovers, and empathizes.
traits.neuroticism_effect: High = emotions hit harder. Low = stoic, muted reactions.
traits.agreeableness_effect: High = mirrors your emotions strongly. Low = resistant, pulls back to neutral when negative.
traits.conscientiousness_effect: High = returns to baseline quickly. Low = moods linger.
traits.extraversion_effect: High = positive, warm baseline. Low = reserved, quieter.

relationship.title: Relationship
relationship.description: The relationship progresses through 4 stages. Progress is one-way — depth never decreases.
relationship.intro: The relationship between you and your assistant evolves through 4 stages. Progress is one-way — depth never decreases, like a real relationship maturing over time.
relationship.orientation: Professional, measured. No assumptions of familiarity.
relationship.exploratory: Shows personality more freely. References past exchanges.
relationship.affective: Personal and direct. Uses humor. Remembers your preferences.
relationship.stable: Trusted companion. Candid, challenges constructively when needed.
relationship.depth_desc: Grows logarithmically with each quality interaction. Never decreases.
relationship.warmth_desc: Active warmth that decays during absence but recovers quickly on contact.
relationship.trust_desc: Bayesian accumulation from interaction quality. Conflict resolution (rupture-repair) gives bonus trust.
relationship.resonance_desc: Computed emotional alignment between you and the assistant. Empathetic matching boosts warmth, honest disagreement in a stable relationship boosts trust.

lifecycle.title: Message lifecycle
lifecycle.intro: Here is what happens at every message, step by step:
lifecycle.pre_desc: Load psyche state → apply decay toward baseline → apply circadian modulation → compile behavioral directives → inject into prompt. The assistant reads its mood, emotions, and relationship directives before generating its answer.
lifecycle.during_desc: The LLM follows the mood, emotion, and relationship directives to adapt its tone. At the end, it self-evaluates: what emotion did this interaction trigger? How positive was the user? This evaluation is hidden from you.
lifecycle.post_desc: Process the self-evaluation: create/reinforce emotion (Neuroticism modulates intensity), push mood in PAD space, apply contagion from user valence (Agreeableness modulates strength), cross-suppress opposite emotions, update relationship metrics, drives and self-efficacy. The new emotional state is sent to the interface.

drives.title: Drives
drives.intro: Drives are internal motivations that evolve with each interaction. They influence how proactive, thorough, and exploratory the assistant is.
drives.curiosity_effect: Explores new angles, asks follow-up questions, suggests tangents.
drives.engagement_effect: More thorough and proactive. In flow — takes initiative.
drives.dynamics: Both drives use a smooth moving average (20% new signal, 80% previous value). They never jump — they drift gradually toward the quality and energy of your exchanges.
drives.efficacy_desc: The assistant tracks its confidence across domains (planning, technical, emotional support, etc.). High confidence means bolder suggestions; low confidence means more caution and thoroughness. Updated after each interaction based on quality feedback.
drives.transitions_desc: The assistant perceives its own emotional shifts between messages. When mood or emotion changes significantly, it receives a narrative transition cue — reunion after absence, valence shifts, arousal changes — guiding a natural, unforced transition.
